story.e:
**The Ring Comes Back**

Haman is dead. The story could end here — but it does not end, and there is a very important reason why.

On that day the king gave the house of Haman to Esther. Then he took off his ring — the ring he had earlier given to Haman, the ring Haman had used to seal his decree — and gave it to Mordecai.

Think about that: **the same ring.** The same seal. The one that signed a people's death now belongs to the man who wants to save them. The ring did not become better or worse. It simply changed hands.

**Esther Asks Again**

And now comes the most important part, the one that is easy to skip.

Esther did not stop. She went in to the king again, fell at his feet, wept, and pleaded: **let him turn aside the decree of Haman.** She asked that the letters be revoked.

Why? Haman is no longer alive. But the **decree** is alive. The letters have already gone out to every province. The appointed day — the thirteenth of the twelfth month — is still ahead.

Esther asked it like this in 8:6: *For how could I bear to see the harm that has come upon my people, and how could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?* This is not a bargain. It means: I cannot live with this.

**The Problem That Cannot Be Solved**

The king's answer is strange until you understand Persian law. He said (8:8): *what is written in the king's name and sealed with his ring cannot be revoked.*

**Cannot be revoked.** This was the same trouble in Daniel's story, when the king spent a whole day trying to get Daniel out and could not (p29, Daniel 6:9). And Memucan said the same thing back in chapter 1 (1:19).

So the king could not erase Haman's decree. He could only write a **second** one beside it.

That is why he said: *write concerning the Jews as you see fit, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring.*

**The Second Decree**

Mordecai wrote it. And look carefully at what it permitted (8:11): that the Jews in every city might **gather and stand for their lives.**

Stand for their lives. Not attack. Not take revenge. But be able **to stand** when that day came and someone attacked them.

These two decrees now stood together in the empire. One said: on this day the Jews may be killed. The other said: on this day the Jews may stand for themselves.

**The City Rejoices**

Mordecai went out from before the king in royal robes: in blue and white, with a great golden crown. And the city of Susa rejoiced and was glad (8:15).

The same city that in 3:15 was *bewildered* when the decree was proclaimed.

And 8:16 says it beautifully: *For the Jews there was light and joy, gladness and honour.*

Then 8:17 says something unusual: many from among the peoples of the land became Jews. But the text also gives the reason, and it is not a beautiful reason: **because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.** The book does not say they understood. It says they were afraid. That is worth reading exactly.

**It Was Reversed**

The day came. And 9:1 sums up the whole book in one word: on the day on which the enemies of the Jews sought to rule over them, **it was reversed.**

The Jews gathered in their cities to stand against those who sought their ruin. There was fighting. Hard fighting. And in the next levels we will talk about exactly what happened, because this is the hardest passage in the book and we are not going to skip it.

But one thing the text states **three times,** and that is no accident: *they did not stretch out their hands to the plunder* (9:10, 9:15, 9:16). They took nothing. It did not become a business.

**Purim**

Mordecai wrote these things and sent letters to all the Jews. He asked that they remember every year.

And now notice **what** is to be done on these days (9:22): *with feasting and joy, with sending gifts to one another and gifts to the poor.*

That is all. Feasting, joy, gifts to one another, and giving to the poor. Not one word about the fighting. The festival does not re-enact the battle — it carries forward the joy and the giving.

It took its name from the **pur,** the lot that Haman cast in 3:7. The festival is named after the thing by which their deaths were drawn by lot — and that became the day of joy.

**The Last Sentence**

The book closes with a chapter shorter than ten lines. And the last sentence is this (10:3): Mordecai was second after the king, great among the Jews; **he sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all his kindred.**

The last word in the Hebrew: *shalom.* Peace.

A book in which God's name never once appears, a book of lots and decrees and banquets and fighting — ends with **peace.**
story.m:
**Why Is There a Chapter 9 at All?**

This is the question that unlocks this part. Haman died at the end of chapter 7. So why are there three more chapters, and why is there fighting in them?

The answer lies in Persian law, and the book warned us about it twice.

**8:1-2 — The Mirror Closes**

On that day the king gave the house of Haman to Esther, and Mordecai came in before the king — because Esther had told **what he was to her** (8:1). This is the very thing 2:10 kept hidden: her kindred. Now it is spoken.

Then the king took off his ring and gave it to Mordecai (8:2).

Compare 3:10: *the king took off his ring and gave it to Haman.* Literally the same gesture. The book replays the scene with a different actor.

This is the book's method: it does not explain, it **reverses.** The same sentence, running the other way.

**8:3-6 — Esther Asks a Third Time**

Esther spoke again, fell at his feet, wept. And now she is not asking for her own life, nor even for her people in general — she is asking for something **legally specific:** that he turn aside the decree of Haman, that the letters be revoked (8:5).

And 8:6 is one of the most human sentences in the book: *how could I bear to see the harm that has come upon my people, and how could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?*

Two questions, the same shape. She does not argue. She says: I cannot watch this.

**8:8 — Irrevocability**

And here comes the book's legal twist. The king says: *what is written in the king's name and sealed with his ring cannot be revoked.*

This is Persian law as the Bible presents it — and we meet it in **three places:**
- **Esther 1:19** — Memucan proposes writing Vashti's banishment down precisely so that it cannot be revoked
- **Daniel 6:9** — Darius laboured all day to rescue Daniel and could not, because the decree was irrevocable (p29)
- **Esther 8:8** — now

So the king **could not** erase Haman's decree. This is not an excuse on his part; it is how the system worked. And everything that happens in chapter 9 follows precisely from it.

**8:9-14 — The Second Decree**

Mordecai wrote the new letter — the book describes in detail how the couriers went on horseback, in haste. (Compare 3:13: couriers went then too. The same roads, a different letter.)

The book here repeats a phrase that has already been heard twice: the letter was written **in the script of every province and the language of every people, and to the Jews in their own script and their own language** (8:9). The same formula stands in 1:22 at Ahasuerus's first decree and in 3:12 at Haman's decree. In its third occurrence there is a new clause: now the Jews are in the list too, in their own language. A people called in 3:8 merely **a scattered people** now appears by name in the empire's official letter.

The day is the same: **the thirteenth of the month of Adar** (8:12), precisely the day Haman appointed in 3:13. The book does not move the day. Everything happens on that same day, only now with two laws.

And now the crucial word. 8:11 permits the Jews to **gather and stand for their lives** — in Hebrew *la'amod al nafsham,* literally: to stand for their souls, their lives.

This is a permission to **defend.** Not an order to attack. It does not even say they must. It says they may.

It matters to see that the second decree did **not cancel** the first. The first decree remained in force. So on that day two laws stood against each other in the same empire.

**8:15-17 — The Reversal Becomes Visible**

Mordecai in royal robes. Susa **rejoiced and was glad** — the same city that was bewildered in 3:15.

8:16 tells the turn in four words: *light and joy, gladness and honour.*

But 8:17 asks for attention. Many from among the peoples of the land became Jews. The Hebrew verb — *mityahadim* — is an unusual form, found nowhere else in the Bible in this shape. And the text **gives the motive: the fear of the Jews.**

This is not a conversion story. The book does not say these people came to understand the God of Israel (whose name the book never even speaks). It says they were afraid. It is more honest to read it that way than to make a pretty story of it.

**9:1-2 — The Word for the Reversal**

9:1 speaks the word that until now only the story's motion had shown: *nahafoch hu* — **it was reversed.** This is the book's own summary of itself.

And 9:2 names whom the Jews gathered against: *those who sought their ruin.*

**9:5-16 — The Hard Passage**

Now comes what has to be spoken about honestly. According to the text the Jews fought, and many died: five hundred in Susa (9:6), the ten sons of Haman (9:7-10), three hundred more on a second day in Susa (9:15), and seventy-five thousand in the provinces (9:16).

These are large numbers. I will not call them small.

Three things have to be seen at once:

**1. What the text itself says about defence.** 8:11 permitted standing; 9:2 says against *those who sought their ruin;* and 9:16 puts it this way: *stood for their lives and had rest from their enemies.* The name the text gives the goal is **rest,** not victory.

**2. What the text says about plunder.** Three times: *they did not stretch out their hands to the plunder* (9:10, 9:15, 9:16). And notice: 8:11 had **permitted** them the plunder. They did not take it. A sentence repeated three times is not an accident — this is the book's own moral note.

**3. What the text does NOT say.** It does not say this may be repeated at any other time. It does not say this is a rule for all ages. It does not say it was right, and it does not say it was wrong. It **reports.** And the festival the book founds out of it is not a festival of fighting but of feasting and giving.

The hard level goes further than this, and it will not hide what remains difficult in this passage either.

**9:20-28 — The Founding of Purim**

Mordecai wrote and sent letters. He asked for four things (9:22):
1. **feasting** — food and joy
2. **joy**
3. **sending gifts to one another**
4. **gifts to the poor** — in Hebrew *mattanot la-evyonim*

That fourth point matters. The celebration does not stop at one's own joy. Jewish tradition counts the command of *mattanot la-evyonim* among the two basic obligations of Purim to this day.

By 9:26 it took its name from the **pur** — the lot Haman cast in 3:7. The festival's name remembers the casting of lots by which a people's death was to be drawn.

**Three Details Worth Noticing**

**9:3** — the officials and administrators of the provinces **helped** the Jews. Why? The verse gives the reason: *because the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them.* Exactly the same construction as in 8:17. Twice the book names fear as the motive, not conviction. It does not prettify its own story.

**9:19** — the Jews of the open villages keep the fourteenth day, while the city of Susa keeps the fifteenth, because there the fighting lasted a day longer. This is why Jewish practice has two dates to this day: Purim and **Shushan Purim.** In this verse the book explains the double calendar of its own festival.

**9:29-32** — and here is something easily missed. Mordecai was not the only one who wrote. **Queen Esther also wrote** a letter, with full authority, and 9:32 closes it: *the decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim, and it was written in the book.*

Esther's last act in the book is not a banquet and not a request. It is a **written document** that enters the record. The girl who was taken in 2:8, and who had to keep silent in 2:10, writes at the end of the book — and her writing remains.

**10:1-3 — The Close**

The book ends with three verses. The king is great, Mordecai second after him. And the last sentence (10:3): *he sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all his kindred.*

That is the book's last word: *shalom.* Not power, not victory, not revenge. **Peace.**
story.h:
**The Question to Start With**

Esther chapter 9 is the place where a reader often stops and asks: how is this all right?

I am not going to dodge the question. But something has to be cleared up first, without which the question cannot even be asked properly.

**The Legal Fact That Explains Everything**

In 8:5 Esther did **not** ask that the Jews be allowed to take up arms. She asked that the decree be **revoked.** That was her request.

The king's answer (8:8): *what is written in the king's name and sealed with his ring cannot be revoked.*

So Esther's request **could not be granted.** The book prepared this twice already: in 1:19 Memucan proposed writing Vashti's banishment down precisely for this reason, and in Daniel 6:9 Darius laboured all day to rescue Daniel and could not (p29).

Chapter 9 follows from that. There is fighting not because anyone wanted fighting, but because the death decree could not be erased, only **a second one** written beside it. And two opposing laws on the same day in the same empire mean fighting.

Anyone who reads chapter 9 as though the Jews could have chosen between fighting and peace attributes to them a choice the book never gives them.

**Exactly What 8:11 Permitted — and Its Difficulty**

The Hebrew of 8:11 permits this: that the Jews *gather and stand for their lives* — *la'amod al nafsham.* Defence.

But the verse continues, and **here lies the hardest translation question in the passage.** The continuation literally contains: to destroy, to kill and to annihilate every army that attacks them — **children and women** — and to take their plunder.

The difficulty: to whom do *children and women* belong?
- **One reading:** to the attacking force — that is, to those who attack them together with their families. On this reading it is a literal echo of 3:13, where Haman's decree wrote the same words about Jewish children and women.
- **Another reading:** to the Jews' own action — that is, it granted them this too.

The Hebrew sentence structure by itself does **not** decide. Translations divide, and modern versions are not uniform. Anyone who says the text certainly means one of them is claiming more than the grammar allows.

What we do know for certain: chapter 9 does **not** say that the Jews killed children or women. Nowhere in 9:5-16 does it say that. 8:11 describes a **permission;** chapter 9 describes an **act.** And on the question of plunder those two demonstrably come apart — which is the next point.

**The Numbers, Which Must Not Be Called Small**

According to the text: five hundred men in the citadel of Susa (9:6), the ten sons of Haman listed by name (9:7-10), three hundred more in Susa on the second day (9:15), and seventy-five thousand in the provinces (9:16).

These are large numbers. The book of Esther exaggerates in several places (the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of 1:1, the hundred and eighty day banquet of 1:4, the fifty-cubit pole of 5:14), and it may exaggerate here too. But that is not an answer. The number does not become small just because I read it as exaggeration.

Four things have to be held at once.

**First: what the text says about the aim.**

Not once but consistently, it uses the words of standing and of rest:
- 8:11: *stand for their lives*
- 9:2: against *those who sought their ruin*
- 9:16: *stood for their lives and had rest from their enemies*

In 9:16 the Hebrew word for the aim is *nuach* — to come to rest. Not *yasha* (to win), not *naqam* (to repay). The text itself names rest, not victory, as the goal.

**Second: the plunder, three times.**

*They did not stretch out their hands to the plunder.* 9:10. 9:15. 9:16.

A biblical text repeats when it wants to stress. And this repetition points exactly where the whole Amalek thread points: to **1 Samuel 15.** There, king Saul came under judgement precisely because he **took** the spoil when he should not have.

So the book called Haman an Agagite (3:1 — and we discussed in p32 that the reference to Amalek is a very probable inference but not the text's stated word), and now, when his descendants fall, the Jews do **not** do what Saul did.

This is the book's moral note on its own story. It does not shout it, but it writes it three times.

**Third: what remains difficult.**

I will not smooth it over. Three things stay hard:

1. **The numbers.** Seventy-five thousand is a very large number, whatever background we are speaking of.

2. **The second day in Susa.** In 9:13 **Esther asked** for the second day. The decree was for one day (8:12). The second day was Esther's request, not the decree's. That is harder to read as pure defence than the first day, and it has to be said.

3. **The hanging of Haman's ten sons** in 9:13-14, after they were already dead. Public display of bodies was the practice of the age, but the practice of an age is not the same as rightness.

**Fourth: what the text does with this, and what it does NOT.**

And here stands the statement we have made several times in this module, at Daniel 6:25 as well (p29): **what the Bible records is not the same as what it teaches.**

The book of Esther **reports** this passage. It does not command it. It does not justify it either. It does not say it was right, and it does not say it was wrong. It writes it in the same cool, uncommenting voice in which it narrated the whole book — the same voice that named no cause in 6:1 and did not correct the king's misreading in 7:8.

And what the book **founds out of it** is the decisive thing. It does not found a battle. It does not found an annual commemoration of the seventy-five thousand. By 9:22 it founds this: **feasting, joy, gifts to one another, and gifts to the poor.**

That is the book's own answer to its own hardest chapter. Anyone who reads fighting out of Purim is reading against 9:22.

**8:17 — What Must Not Be Prettified**

One more honesty. By 8:17 many from among the peoples of the land became Jews. A lovely sentence — until we read its end: **because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.**

The Hebrew verb is *mityahadim,* an unusual form, found only here in the Bible. It means: made themselves Jews, or professed themselves Jews — the exact boundary of the meaning is disputed.

But the text **gives** the motive, and it is not conviction but fear. To teach this as a conversion story is to do exactly what this module tries throughout to avoid: adding to the text.

**The God Who Is Not Named in the Book**

Now, at the end of the book, it is worth looking back.

God's name appears **not once** in the Hebrew book of Esther. There is no prayer, no temple, no law, no sacrifice. In 4:16 there is fasting — but the text mentions no prayer (p33).

Ancient readers felt this so strongly that Greek Esther (the Septuagint text) **inserted** the missing prayers: the prayer of Mordecai and the long prayer of Esther. These are present in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; they are absent from the Hebrew. This is not a secret but a well-documented fact.

Why did the canon keep the silent version?

One possible answer — and it is only a possible answer, not the book's stated claim: because there are times when a person does not see God in their own story. When there is no pillar of fire, no burning bush, no voice from heaven. Only a sleepless night, an old record read aloud, and a series of things that follow one another strangely well.

The book does not claim God was behind them. But it does not claim he was not. It leaves empty the place where the explanation would go. And anyone who has read 4:14 — *who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?* — knows that this book does not resolve its questions (p33).

**A Small Divergence in 9:24-25**

Mordecai's letter summarises the story — and the summary is not exactly the same as the narrative. By 9:25 the king commanded that Haman and his sons be hanged on the pole. But by 7:9-10 the king said *hang him on it* — at Harbona's suggestion, without Esther asking; and the hanging of the sons happened in 9:13-14 at Esther's request.

This is not a contradiction but a **summary.** Still, it is worth noticing: a letter that founds a festival already compresses and simplifies. The book kept both: the detailed narrative and the shortened official version. Anyone who reads only 9:24-25 knows less than someone who also reads chapters 7 and 9.

**A Fact Not Often Mentioned: Esther and Qumran**

Among the Dead Sea Scrolls — in the Qumran caves, where fragments of almost every book of the Hebrew Bible were found — **Esther is the only book from which nothing at all turned up.**

This is a fact, not an opinion. What it means is disputed, and there are at least three explanations:
- **chance** — the survival of fragments is capricious anyway
- **the community did not use it** — because the book contains no name of God, no temple, and Purim is not among the festivals of the Torah
- **the calendar** — the Qumran community used a different calendar, and the date of Purim did not fit it

We do not know which is right. But anyone who says this proves the book was composed late is claiming more than the find allows; and so is anyone who says it means nothing.

**The Question of Historicity — Both Sides**

Honestly: this question is not settled, and this part cannot be written in a way that silences one side.

**What makes it difficult:**
- Greek historiography names Xerxes's (Ahasuerus's) wife as **Amestris,** not Esther or Vashti (Herodotus VII.61, IX.109-112).
- No Persian source known to us mentions Esther, Mordecai or Haman.
- The names resemble Babylonian divine names strikingly: **Mordecai** — *Marduk,* **Esther** — *Ishtar.* (Though 2:7 gives Esther a second name as well: **Hadassah,** which in Hebrew means myrtle. So the book itself knows of two names.)
- The hundred and twenty-seven provinces (1:1) are more than the Persian inscriptions know of (those speak of twenty to thirty satrapies, though the number of smaller administrative units may have differed).

**What speaks for the book:**
- The Persian court detail is accurate: the seven counsellors (1:14; cf. Ezra 7:14), the postal system (3:13; 8:10), the book of records (2:23; 6:1), the rules of prostration before the king, the names of court offices.
- Many Persian loanwords appear in the Hebrew text, used correctly (*patsegen, achashtaran, dat, partemim*).
- The name **Mordecai** has turned up in one form on a Persepolis economic tablet (*Marduka*) — but whether it is the same man cannot be known, and the name was common.

What can honestly be said from this? That the book **knows the Persian world well,** but we cannot confirm its main characters from Persian sources. That is not the same as saying they did not live. And it is not the same as saying they did.

It is the same situation as Darius the Mede in p29: the question is open, and anyone who closes it in either direction is reading their own conviction rather than the text.

**A Custom Worth Knowing About — Which Is Not in the Bible**

In the synagogue practice of Purim the book of Esther (the *megillah*) is read aloud, and when Haman's name is spoken the congregation makes noise to **drown it out.** This is a fine and ancient custom — but it is **not in the Bible.** 9:22 prescribes four things: feasting, joy, gifts and giving to the poor. The noise-making is later tradition. It is worth knowing the difference between the two.

**The Book's Last Word**

10:3 closes it: Mordecai was second after the king, great among the Jews; *he sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all his kindred.*

The last word in the Hebrew is *shalom.* Peace.

A book with lots in it, and a death decree, and a chapter that has to be spoken about honestly — ends with peace. Not because everything is all right. But because someone, in the end, **sought the good of his people.**

**What Comes Next?**

With this the book of Esther ends, and the time of exile ends. From p36 they go home: Ezra, Nehemiah, the rebuilding of the temple, the walls, and the prophets who spoke to those who returned. A different tone, different questions. But the same method: we look at what the text says, and we look at what it does not.

story.e:
**Hetven év után**

Az Eszter könyvében egyetlen egyszer sem volt kimondva, hogy Isten tett valamit. Minden fordulat egyszerűen **megtörtént,** és az olvasóra volt bízva, hogy mit gondol róla.

Most nyisd ki az Ezsdrás könyvét, és olvasd el az első mondatot:

*Círus perzsa király első évében az Úr felindította Círus lelkét.*

Kimondva. Egyértelműen. Két szomszédos könyv, két teljesen más hangnem — és a Biblia mind a kettőt megőrizte.

**A rendelet, amely haza engedett**

Círus, az új nagy király, kihirdette az egész birodalmában: *Aki közületek való, legyen vele az Istene, menjen fel Jeruzsálembe, és építse az Úrnak, Izráel Istenének házát* (1:3).

És még valamit: akik otthon maradnak, **segítsenek** azoknak, akik elmennek — ezüsttel, arannyal, vagyonnal, állatokkal (1:4).

Aztán Círus kiadta a templom **eszközeit** is, az arany- és ezüsttálakat, amelyeket Nebukadneccar elvitt Jeruzsálemből (1:7). Hetven éve álltak egy babiloni raktárban. Most hazamennek.

**Akinek Isten felindította a lelkét**

És most figyelj egy nagyon pontos mondatra (1:5): *fölkeltek Júda és Benjámin családfői, a papok és a léviták, mindenki, akinek az Isten felindította a lelkét.*

**Mindenki, akinek.** Vagyis nem mindenki. Sokan maradtak. Babilonban addigra nagy zsidó közösség élt, házakkal, kertekkel, munkával — ahogy Jeremiás tanácsolta nekik (Jeremiás 29:5). Nekik Jeruzsálem egy romváros volt, amit sosem láttak.

A szöveg **nem ítéli el** azokat, akik maradtak. Egy szóval sem. Ezt jó pontosan észrevenni.

**Negyvenkétezer ember**

Akik mentek, egy hosszú listát kaptak. Az Ezsdrás 2. fejezete nevekkel, családokkal, városokkal teli. A végén egy szám: **negyvenkétezer-háromszázhatvan** (2:64).

A listában van egy szomorú bejegyzés is (2:59): voltak, akik feljöttek, **de nem tudták megmutatni a családjukat és a származásukat.** A fogság hosszú volt. Iratok elvesztek. Emlékek összekeveredtek.

És a szöveg nem küldi el őket. Nem is dönt róluk. Azt mondja: ez a kérdés maradjon nyitva, amíg egy pap nem tud dönteni róla (2:63). **Nyitva hagy egy kérdést.** Ezt a könyv nyugodtan megteszi.

**Először az oltár**

Megérkeztek. És most mit kezdenek egy romvárossal?

Nem a falat építették fel. Nem a házakat. Nem a templomot.

Az első, amit megépítettek, egy **oltár** volt (3:2) — egy kőrakás, ahol áldozatot lehet bemutatni. És a 3:6 pontosan megadja, hogy ez mit jelentett: *elkezdtek égőáldozatot vinni az Úrnak, de az Úr templomának alapja még nem volt letéve.*

Nem volt templom. Csak oltár, nyílt ég alatt, a romok között. És már kezdték.

De a 3:3 hozzátesz valamit, amit nem szépít meg: *felállították az oltárt a helyén, mert **félelem** volt rajtuk a környező népek miatt.*

Nem diadalmenetben kezdtek. Félve kezdtek.

**Az alapkő**

Aztán jött a nagy nap. Letették a templom alapját.

A papokat trombitákkal, a lévitákat cintányérokkal odaállították, Dávid régi rendje szerint (3:10). És énekeltek — azt az éneket, amit Izráel évszázadok óta énekelt:

*Mert ő jó, mert örökké tart az ő szeretete Izráel iránt* (3:11).

És az egész nép **nagy örömmel kiáltott.**

**De nem mindenki kiáltott**

És itt jön a rész szíve, és ez az a hely, amiért érdemes volt eljutni idáig.

Voltak ott idős emberek. Papok, léviták, családfők, akik már **látták az első házat** — Salamon templomát, mielőtt Nebukadneccar lerombolta. Hetven éve. Gyerekkorukban.

Ők látták ezt az alapot, és **hangosan sírtak** (3:12).

Miért? Mert kicsi volt. Mert emlékeztek valami nagyobbra. Mert tudták, mi veszett el.

És a többiek — a fiatalok, akik csak hallottak az első házról — **örömmel kiáltottak.** Mert számukra ez volt a legnagyobb dolog, ami valaha történt.

**Egy hangon**

És most olvasd el a 3:13-at, mert ez a Biblia egyik legszebb verse:

*Úgyhogy a nép nem tudta megkülönböztetni az örömkiáltás szavát a nép sírásának szavától, mert a nép nagy kiáltással kiáltott, és a hang messzire elhallatszott.*

Nem lehetett szétválasztani. Aki kívülről hallgatta, egyetlen nagy hangot hallott, és nem tudta volna megmondani, hogy öröm-e vagy gyász.

És itt a legfontosabb: a szöveg **nem javítja ki a sírókat.** Nem mondja, hogy hálátlanok. Nem mondja, hogy nem értik, mi történik. Nem mondja, hogy abba kellene hagyni.

Nem mondja meg, melyik hang volt a helyes.

Mert néha mind a kettő a helyes. Lehet ugyanabban a percben örülni egy kezdetnek és sírni azért, ami elveszett. A Biblia tudja ezt, és nem kéri, hogy válassz.
story.m:
**Két szomszédos könyv, két módszer**

Ha az Eszter könyvét épp most fejeztük be, akkor az Ezsdrás első mondata szinte megdöbbentő:

*Círus perzsa király első évében az Úr felindította Círus lelkét, hogy beteljesedjék az Úr szava, amelyet Jeremiás által mondott* (1:1).

Az Eszter könyve harminchárom oldalon át **egyszer sem** nevezte meg Istent, és egyszer sem mondott okot a fordulatokra. A 6:1 még az álmatlan éjszakánál sem adott alanyt: *elment a király álma* (p34).

Az Ezsdrás 1:1 a mondat első felében megnevezi a cselekvőt, a második felében pedig a célt is: Jeremiás szava.

Egyik módszer sem jobb a másiknál. A kánon mind a kettőt megőrizte — egymás mellett.

**A hetven év, és ami nehéz benne**

Melyik szóra utal az 1:1? Jeremiás kétszer beszélt hetven évről:
- **Jeremiás 25:11-12** — ez a föld pusztasággá lesz, és ezek a népek a babiloni királyt szolgálják hetven évig
- **Jeremiás 29:10** — amikor betelik a hetven év, meglátogatlak titeket, és visszahozlak erre a helyre

És most a becsületes rész: **a hetven év kiszámolása nem egyértelmű,** és a szöveg nem adja meg a számítást.

Két lehetséges számolás, mind a kettőnek vannak támogatói:
- **Kr. e. 605-től** (az első elhurcolás, Dániel is akkor került el, p24) **538-ig** (Círus rendelete) — ez körülbelül 67 év
- **Kr. e. 586-tól** (a templom lerombolása) **516-ig** (a második templom elkészülte) — ez körülbelül 70 év

Mind a kettő védhető. Lehet, hogy a hetven kerek szám, amit a Biblia máshol is így használ (egy emberélet hossza a Zsoltárok 90:10-ben). Lehet, hogy pontos szám egy olyan kezdő- és végpontra, amit nem nevez meg.

Nem tudjuk biztosan. És aki azt mondja, hogy pontosan tudja, többet mond, mint amit a szöveg ad.

**Círus — és amit nem szabad belemagyarázni**

Az 1:2-ben Círus így beszél: *Az Úr, az ég Istene nekem adta a föld minden királyságát, és ő bízott meg engem, hogy építsek neki házat Jeruzsálemben.*

Szép mondat. De mit jelent?

Van egy tárgy, amiből sokat megtudhatunk: a **Círus-henger.** Egy agyaghenger, amelyet 1879-ben találtak Babilonban, és ma a londoni British Museumban látható. Círus saját szövege van rajta.

És mit ír? Hogy Círus visszaállította a lerombolt szentélyeket, hazaengedte az elhurcolt népeket, és — figyelj — hogy mindezt **Marduk,** Babilon főistene bízta rá, aki kiválasztotta őt és a kezébe adta a várost.

Vagyis ugyanazt a mondatot, amit az Ezsdrás 1:2 Izráel Istenéről ír, Círus **Mardukról** is leíratta.

Ebből két dolog következik egyszerre:

**1. A Biblia képe a politikáról pontos.** Círus valóban ilyen politikát folytatott: helyreállította a helyi szentélyeket, és az illető nép istenének a nevében tette. Ez külső forrásból igazolt. Ez komoly megerősítés.

**2. De az Ezsdrás 1:2-t NEM szabad Círus személyes hitének olvasni.** A Biblia nem mondja, hogy Círus Izráel Istenében hitt. Nem mondja, hogy megtért. Nem mondja, hogy csak nekik tette.

Egy jó döntés nem ugyanaz, mint egy hitvallás. Ezt pontosan kell olvasni. (Ézsaiás 45:1 egyébként **felkentnek** nevezi Círust, és a 45:4-5 hozzáteszi: *bár nem ismertél engem.* A Biblia maga mondja ki, hogy Círus nem ismerte Izráel Istenét.)

**A második kivonulás**

Az 1:4 egy furcsa dolgot kér: a helyben maradók **segítsék** a hazatérőket ezüsttel, arannyal, vagyonnal, állatokkal.

Ez nem véletlen megfogalmazás. A 2Mózes 12:35-36-ban ugyanez történt: amikor Izráel kijött Egyiptomból, az egyiptomiak **ezüstöt és aranyat** adtak nekik.

Az Ezsdrás könyve a hazatérést egy **második kivonulásként** mutatja be. Ugyanaz a mozdulat: kijönni egy birodalomból, ajándékokkal megrakva, egy ígéret felé.

**A lista, és a szám, ami nem jön ki**

Az Ezsdrás 2 egy hosszú névsor. A végén: *az egész gyülekezet együtt negyvenkétezer-háromszázhatvan volt* (2:64).

Most jön egy becsületes nehézség, amit nem lehet elhallgatni.

Ha összeadod a fejezetben felsorolt egyes számokat, körülbelül **huszonkilencezer-nyolcszáz** jön ki. Nem negyvenkétezer.

És van még egy dolog: ugyanez a lista **másodszor is** szerepel a Bibliában, a **Nehemiás 7-ben** — és ott sok egyes szám **más,** miközben a végösszeg ugyanaz: negyvenkétezer-háromszázhatvan.

Mit lehet erre mondani?

Több magyarázat van, és egyik sincs bizonyítva:
- a végösszeg olyanokat is tartalmaz, akiket a lista nem tételez (nőket, szolgákat, a 2:59-ben említett bizonytalan származásúakat)
- a héber számjegyek írásmódja miatt a másolásnál könnyen változtak a számok
- a két lista két különböző időpontban készült nyilvántartás

De egy dolgot érdemes észrevenni: **a hagyomány mind a két listát megőrizte.** Nem simította ki. Nem harmonizálta. Aki a Bibliát összeolvasta, látta a különbséget, és **benne hagyta.**

**A kérdés, amit nyitva hagytak**

A 2:59 egy nehéz helyzetről szól: voltak, akik feljöttek, de nem tudták megmutatni a származásukat. A fogság hetven éve alatt elvesztek az iratok.

És mit tesz a szöveg? A 2:63 szerint: a döntést elhalasztották, amíg egy pap az **urimmal és a tummimmal** (a főpapi döntéshozás eszközeivel) nem dönt róla.

Vagyis **nem döntöttek.** Nem zárták ki őket, és nem is vették fel őket teljes joggal. Nyitva hagyták.

Ez a könyv módszere is: egy nyitott kérdést nyitva hagyni becsületesebb, mint gyorsan lezárni.

**Először az oltár, félelemben**

A 3:1-ben a nép **egy emberként** gyűlt össze Jeruzsálembe. Aztán Jésua (a főpap) és Zerubbábel (Dávid házából való vezető) megépítették az oltárt, *ahogyan meg van írva Mózes törvényében* (3:2).

A 3:3 pedig kimondja az okot is: *mert félelem volt rajtuk a környező népek miatt.*

Ez nem diadalmenet. A szöveg maga nevezi meg a félelmet — ahogy az Eszter 8:17 és 9:3 is félelmet nevezett meg (p35). Ezek a könyvek nem csinálnak hősi történetet abból, ami félelemben indult.

És a 3:6 a legfontosabb részlet: *elkezdtek égőáldozatot vinni az Úrnak, **de az Úr templomának alapja még nem volt letéve.***

Oltár előbb, templom utóbb. Az istentisztelet nem várta meg az épületet.

**Az alapkő és a két hang**

A 3:10-ben letették az alapot, és odaállították a papokat trombitákkal, a lévitákat cintányérokkal, *Dávid rendelése szerint.*

És énekeltek (3:11): *Mert ő jó, mert örökké tart az ő szeretete Izráel iránt.*

Ez a refrén nem új. Ez a **136. zsoltár** refrénje, amely huszonhat versen át ismétlődik; ott van a 118. zsoltár elején és végén, és az 1Krónikák 16:34-ben is. Egy nép, amely hetven évig nem énekelhette ezt a templomban, most újra elkezdi — ugyanazzal a sorral.

És a 3:12: *sok idős pap, lévita és családfő, akik látták az első házat, hangosan sírtak.*

A **Haggeus 2:3** ugyanerre a veszteségre kérdez rá, nagyjából ugyanabban az időben: *Ki van még közöttetek, aki látta ezt a házat az előbbi dicsőségében?* Haggeus ott választ is ad (2:9: ennek a háznak nagyobb lesz a dicsősége).

De az **Ezsdrás 3 nem ad választ.** Nem vigasztal. Nem magyaráz. Csak leírja a két hangot, és hozzáteszi (3:13), hogy nem lehetett őket megkülönböztetni.

**Amit a szöveg NEM mond**

Négy dolgot nem mond a 3:12-13:
1. Nem mondja, hogy az idősek hibáztak.
2. Nem mondja, hogy a sírásuk hitetlenség volt.
3. Nem mondja, hogy abba kellene hagyni.
4. **Nem mondja meg, melyik hang volt a helyes.**

Egyszerűen hagyja, hogy mind a kettő ott legyen. És hagyja, hogy a hang **messzire elhallatsszon** — mindkettő benne.
story.h:
**Mi változik, amikor a fogság véget ér?**

Ez a rész a Bibliaút egyik fordulópontja. Eddig egy nép elvesztett mindent, és megtanulta, hogyan éljen idegen földön. Mostantól visszamegy — és megtudja, hogy a visszamenés nem ugyanaz, mint a visszakapás.

Négy dolgot kell pontosan megbeszélni: a hetven évet, Círust, a számokat, és a két hangot.

**1. Az Ezsdrás 1:1 — amikor a Biblia kimondja az okot**

Közvetlenül az Eszter könyve után (p31-p35) ez a mondat szinte sokkol:

*Az Úr felindította Círus lelkét.*

A héber ige *hé'ír* — felkelteni, felindítani; a 1:5-ben ugyanez áll a hazatérőkről is. Ugyanaz az ige Círusra és Isten népére. A szöveg nem tesz közéjük különbséget abban, hogy ki indította őket.

Hasonlítsd össze az Eszter könyvével. Ott:
- Nem szerepel Isten neve (p35)
- A 6:1-ben a király álmatlanságának **nincs megadva oka** — a héber *nádödá* alanytalan (p34)
- A 4:14 **kérdés,** nem állítás: *ki tudja?* (p33)

Itt pedig az első félmondatban megnevezi a cselekvőt.

Ez nem azt jelenti, hogy az egyik könyv jobb. Azt jelenti, hogy **a Bibliában van kimondott és van hallgató elbeszélés is,** és a kánon mind a kettőt megőrizte. Van, amikor az ember látja Isten kezét a történetében, és van, amikor csak utólag, és van, amikor soha. Mind a három állapotra van könyv.

**2. A hetven év — és a számolás, amit nem a szöveg végez el**

Az 1:1 Jeremiásra utal. Két hely van:
- **Jeremiás 25:11-12** — a föld pusztasággá lesz, és ezek a népek Babilon királyát szolgálják hetven évig; és a hetven év betelte után megítélem Babilon királyát
- **Jeremiás 29:10** — amikor betelik Babilonra a hetven év, meglátogatlak titeket

A 2Krónikák 36:21 is erre utal, és hozzáteszi egy másik szempontot: a föld **nyugalmi éveit** töltötte be (a szombatévek gondolata a 3Mózes 26:34-35-ből).

A nehézség: honnan hová számolunk?

**Három javaslat, mind a hármat képviselik tudósok:**

| Kezdet | Vég | Hossz | Mi az esemény |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kr. e. 605 | 539/538 | kb. 67 ev | elso elhurcolas (Dan 1:1) - Cirus gyozelme |
| Kr. e. 597 | 538 | kb. 59 ev | Jojakin elhurcolasa - a rendelet |
| Kr. e. 586 | 516 | kb. 70 ev | a templom lerombolasa - a masodik templom elkeszulte |

A harmadik adja ki a legpontosabban a hetvenet, de a 2Krónikák 36 inkább az elsőre vagy a másodikra látszik gondolni, és az Ezsdrás 1:1 Círus első évéhez kapcsolja.

Van egy negyedik lehetőség is, amit érdemes megfontolni: a **hetven kerek szám.** A Bibliában a hetven gyakran teljességet jelöl — egy emberélet hossza a Zsoltárok 90:10-ben, hetven nemzetség az 1Mózes 10-ben, hetven vén a 2Mózes 24:1-ben. Ha így olvassuk, a hetven év azt mondja: **egy teljes emberélet.** Aki elment, nem jött vissza. Aki visszajött, ott született.

A szöveg a számítást nem adja meg. Ez nem baj — csak nem szabad belőle bizonyosságot csinálni.

**3. Círus — a Círus-henger, és a határ, amit nem szabad átlépni**

Ez a rész legfontosabb pontossága.

**A tárgy.** 1879-ben Hormuzd Rassam Babilonban megtalált egy agyaghengert akkád nyelvű felirattal. Ma a British Museumban van, és **Círus-hengerként** ismert. Kr. e. 539 körülre datálják.

**Mi van rajta.** Círus elbeszéli, hogy Babilon bevétele után:
- helyreállította a lerombolt szentélyeket
- visszavitte a kiszorított isteneket a saját helyükre
- hazaengedte az elhurcolt lakosságot
- és mindezt **Marduk** bízta rá, aki kiválasztotta őt és a kezébe adta a várost

Vagyis a mondat szerkezete, amit az Ezsdrás 1:2-ben olvasunk — *az Úr, az ég Istene... ő bízott meg engem* —, egy **ismert perzsa udvari formula,** amelyet Círus más népek isteneivel is használt.

**Mit jelent ez, és mit nem?**

**Ami megerősítés:** a Biblia által leírt politika valódi. Nem a bibliai szerző találta ki, hogy egy perzsa király hazaengedi a népeket és templomot építtet nekik az ő istenük nevében. Ez dokumentált perzsa gyakorlat. Ez komoly és fontos.

**Ami viszont nem következik:** nem következik, hogy Círus Izráel Istenében hitt. És a Biblia nem is állítja ezt.

Sőt — a Biblia maga mondja ki az ellenkezőjét. Ézsaiás 45:1 Círust **az Úr felkentjének** (héberül *másíach*) nevezi, ami a Bibliában egyedülálló egy idegen királyra. De a 45:4-5 azonnal hozzáteszi: *neveden nevezlek... **bár nem ismertél engem.***

A Biblia tehát egyszerre mondja, hogy Isten használta Círust, és hogy Círus nem ismerte őt.

Ez egy fontos gondolat, és nem csak Círusról szól: **valaki tehet jót, lehet eszköz valami nagyban, és közben nem kell neki hitvallást tennie.** És fordítva: egy jó döntésből nem lehet visszafejteni, hogy valaki mit hisz.

Aki az Ezsdrás 1:2-t Círus megtéréseként tanítja, az ellentmond az Ézsaiás 45:4-nek.

**4. A számok — a nehézség, amit a hagyomány benne hagyott**

A 2:64 azt mondja: az egész gyülekezet **42 360.**

Két probléma van, és egyik sem titok:

**Az első: a részletek összege kisebb.** Ha összeadjuk az Ezsdrás 2-ben felsorolt csoportokat, körülbelül **29 818** jön ki. A hiányzó bő tizenkétezer nincs megmagyarázva a fejezetben.

**A második: a Nehemiás 7 ugyanezt a listát adja — más részletekkel.** A Nehemiás 7:6-72 szinte szó szerint ugyanaz a névsor, de **sok egyes szám eltér** (például Aráh fiai: Ezsd 2:5 szerint 775, Neh 7:10 szerint 652). A Nehemiás 7 részleteinek összege körülbelül **31 089.** És a végösszeg mind a két helyen ugyanaz: **42 360.**

**Magyarázatok, és hogy melyik mennyire áll:**

1. **A végösszeg többet foglal magába, mint a tételek.** A lista férfiakat sorol fel családok és városok szerint; a végösszeg tartalmazhat nőket, a fel nem sorolt törzsek tagjait, és a 2:59-ben említett bizonytalan származásúakat. Ez a legelterjedtebb magyarázat, de a szöveg nem mondja ki.
2. **Másolási eltérések.** A héber számokat betűkkel is írhatták, és a hasonló betűk könnyen felcserélődhettek. Ez megmagyarázza az Ezsdrás és a Nehemiás közti különbségeket, de nem magyarázza meg, miért egyezik mégis a végösszeg.
3. **Két különböző nyilvántartás.** Lehet, hogy az egyik az induláskor, a másik a megérkezés után készült, és közben változott a létszám.

Egyik sem bizonyított. A becsületes válasz: **nem tudjuk.**

De van itt valami, ami önmagában tanulságos. A két listát a hagyomány **nem simította ki.** Ott vannak egymás mellett a Bibliában, eltérő számokkal. Aki összeszerkesztette ezeket a könyveket, látta a különbséget — és **nem javította ki.** Ez azt mondja a Biblia keletkezéséről, hogy a megőrzés fontosabb volt, mint a sima felszín.

**5. A 2:59-63 — amikor a szöveg nem dönt**

Voltak, akik feljöttek Babilonból, de nem tudták igazolni a származásukat (2:59). Közöttük papi családok is (2:61-62).

Mi történik velük? A 2:63: a vezető azt mondta, hogy ne egyenek a szent dolgokból, amíg nem **áll elő egy pap az urimmal és a tummimmal.**

Az urim és a tummim a főpapi döntéshozás eszközei voltak (2Mózes 28:30; 1Sámuel 14:41; 28:6). És a bibliai időrendben a fogság után **nincs feljegyzés** arról, hogy használták volna őket.

Vagyis a 2:63 gyakorlatilag ezt jelenti: a kérdés **nyitva marad, határozatlan időre.** Nem zárták ki őket a népből, és nem is kaptak teljes papi jogokat.

Ez nem kibúvó, hanem döntés: egy bizonytalan kérdést nem lezárni, hanem nyitva tartani. A Biblia máshol is ezt teszi (az Eszter 4:14 kérdése, p33; Dániel 12:8-9 lepecsételt könyve, p30).

**6. Az oltár előbb, mint a templom — és a félelem**

A 3:1-ben a nép **egy emberként** (héberül *ke-ís echád*) gyűlt össze — ugyanaz a fordulat, mint a Bírák 20:1-ben és a Nehemiás 8:1-ben.

A hetedik hónap nem véletlen: ebben a hónapban van a kürtzengés napja, a nagy engesztelőnap és a sátoros ünnep (3Mózes 23:23-43). A visszatérők a naptár legsűrűbb hónapjában kezdtek.

És az oltárt építették meg először, *ahogyan meg van írva Mózes törvényében* (3:2). Nem a falat, nem a házakat, nem a templomot. A 3:6 kimondja: *elkezdtek égőáldozatot vinni az Úrnak, de az Úr templomának alapja még nem volt letéve.*

De a 3:3 megadja a körülményt is, és ezt nem szabad kihagyni: *mert **félelem** volt rajtuk a környező népek miatt.*

A szöveg nem csinál hőstörténetet ebből. Ugyanúgy nem, mint az Eszter 8:17-ben és 9:3-ban, ahol a félelem volt a megnevezett motívum (p35). Ezek a könyvek pontosak abban, hogy mi mozgatta az embereket — és a félelem gyakrabban szerepel, mint a diadal.

**7. A két hang — a rész szíve**

A 3:10-11-ben letették az alapot, a papok trombitával, a léviták cintányérral, Dávid rendje szerint, és énekelték: *mert ő jó, mert örökké tart az ő szeretete Izráel iránt.*

Ez a refrén a 136. zsoltár gerince (huszonhat versben), a 118. zsoltár kerete, és az 1Krónikák 16:34 is idézi. A szöveg nem új éneket ad nekik. A **régit** adja vissza.

És aztán a 3:12. Az idősek, akik **látták az első házat,** hangosan sírtak.

Mennyi idősnek kellett lennie valakinek? Ha a templom Kr. e. 586-ban pusztult el, és az alapkőletétel 536 körül volt, akkor annak, aki emlékezett rá, legalább ötvenöt-hatvan évesnek kellett lennie. Gyerekkorukban látták. Hetven évvel azelőtt.

Mit láttak most? Egy alapot. Kisebbet. Szegényesebbet.

A **Haggeus 2:3** ugyanerre a pillanatra (vagy nagyon közel hozzá) kérdez rá: *Ki van még közöttetek, aki látta ezt a házat az előbbi dicsőségében? És milyennek látjátok most?* Haggeus ad is választ: a 2:9 szerint *ennek az új háznak nagyobb lesz a dicsősége, mint az előbbinek.*

De az Ezsdrás 3 **nem ad választ.** Nem idézi Haggeust. Nem vigasztal. Nem magyaráz. Csak leírja.

És a 3:13: *a nép nem tudta megkülönböztetni az örömkiáltás szavát a nép sírásának szavától.*

A héber szerkezet hangsúlyos: nem tudták *lehakkír* — felismerni, azonosítani. Egyetlen hang volt.

**Amit a 3:12-13 NEM mond — és miért fontos**

Öt dolgot nem mond, és mindegyik hiányzás szándékos:

1. **Nem mondja, hogy az idősek hibáztak.** Egyetlen szó sincs arról, hogy a sírásuk helytelen lett volna.
2. **Nem mondja, hogy hitetlenek voltak.** Nem mondja, hogy ha jobban bíznának, nem sírnának.
3. **Nem mondja, hogy abba kellene hagyni.** Senki nem csitítja le őket.
4. **Nem mondja, hogy a fiatalok örömében volt valami hiba.** Az ő kiáltásuk is ott van, ugyanolyan jogon.
5. **Nem mondja meg, melyik hang volt a helyes.**

Ez a hiányzás a vers tanítása. Mert ha a szöveg eldöntötte volna, akkor valakinek hazudnia kellene arról, hogy mit érez.

Ez azokhoz is beszél, akik olvassák. Van, hogy valaki egy jó dologban áll — új iskola, új otthon, új kezdet —, és közben fáj neki az, ami elveszett. És néha azt várják tőle, hogy válasszon: vagy örülj, vagy szomorkodj.

Az Ezsdrás 3:13 nem kéri ezt. Azt mondja: **a két hang összeért, és a hang messzire elhallatszott.**

Mind a kettő benne volt.

**Mi jön?**

A p37-ben a munka megáll. Nem azért, mert elfáradtak — hanem mert jön valaki, aki szépen kér, és a kérés mögött más van. És ott jön be Haggeus és Zakariás, a két próféta, akik ebbe a megállásba beszéltek bele.

verse.text: Úgyhogy a nép nem tudta megkülönböztetni az örömkiáltás szavát a nép sírásának szavától, mert a nép nagy kiáltással kiáltott, és a hang messzire elhallatszott.

e.q: Kinek a lelkét indította fel az Úr az 1:1-ben?
e.qe: Whose spirit did the LORD stir in 1:1?

v.t: Círus perzsa király első évében az Úr felindította Círus lelkét, hogy beteljesedjék az Úr szava, amelyet Jeremiás által mondott; és Círus kihirdette az egész országában.

ve.t: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus, so that the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah might be fulfilled; and Cyrus made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom.

e.q: Mit kellett Círus szerint építeni Jeruzsálemben?
e.qe: What was to be built in Jerusalem, by Cyrus?

v.t: Így szól Círus, Perzsia királya: Az Úr, az ég Istene nekem adta a föld minden királyságát, és ő bízott meg engem, hogy építsek neki házat Jeruzsálemben.

ve.t: Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house in Jerusalem.

e.q: Mit mondott Círus azoknak, akik felmennek?
e.qe: What did Cyrus say to those who would go up?
oe: May his God be with him

v.t: Aki közületek való, legyen vele az Istene, menjen fel Jeruzsálembe, és építse az Úrnak, Izráel Istenének házát.

ve.t: Whoever is among you, may his God be with him, let him go up to Jerusalem and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel.

e.q: Kik keltek fel, hogy menjenek?
e.qe: Who rose up to go?
o: Akinek az Isten felindította a lelkét
oe: Everyone whose spirit God had stirred

v.t: Akkor fölkeltek Júda és Benjámin családfői, a papok és a léviták, mindenki, akinek az Isten felindította a lelkét, hogy menjen és építse az Úr házát.

ve.t: Then the heads of the families of Judah and Benjamin rose up, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred, to go up and build the house of the LORD.

e.q: Mit adott ki Círus király?
e.qe: What did king Cyrus bring out?
oe: The vessels of the house of the LORD

v.t: Círus király kiadta az Úr házának eszközeit is, amelyeket Nebukadneccar elvitt Jeruzsálemből.

ve.t: King Cyrus also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD, which Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem.

e.q: Mit építettek meg először?
e.qe: What did they build first?

v.t: És fölkelt Jésua és Zerubbábel, és megépítették Izráel Istenének oltárát, hogy égőáldozatokat vigyenek rá, ahogyan meg van írva Mózes törvényében.

ve.t: And Jeshua and Zerubbabel rose up and built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the law of Moses.

e.q: Miért állították fel az oltárt a 3:3 szerint?
e.qe: Why did they set up the altar, by 3:3?
o: Mert félelem volt rajtuk a környező népek miatt
oe: Because fear was upon them from the surrounding peoples

v.t: Felállították az oltárt a helyén, mert félelem volt rajtuk a környező népek miatt; és égőáldozatokat vittek rá az Úrnak, reggel és este.

en.name: Joy and Weeping in One Sound

story.e:
**After Seventy Years**

In the book of Esther, not once was it said that God had done anything. Every turn simply **happened,** and it was left to the reader what to make of it.

Now open the book of Ezra and read the first sentence:

*In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus.*

Said outright. Unmistakably. Two neighbouring books, two completely different voices — and the Bible kept both.

**The Decree That Let Them Go Home**

Cyrus, the new great king, made a proclamation throughout his empire: *Whoever is among you, may his God be with him, let him go up to Jerusalem and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel* (1:3).

And one more thing: those who stay behind should **help** those who go — with silver, gold, goods and animals (1:4).

Then Cyrus also brought out the **vessels** of the temple, the gold and silver bowls that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem (1:7). For seventy years they had stood in a Babylonian storeroom. Now they were going home.

**Everyone Whose Spirit God Had Stirred**

And now notice a very precise sentence (1:5): *the heads of the families of Judah and Benjamin rose up, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred.*

**Everyone whose.** Which means: not everyone. Many stayed. By then a large Jewish community lived in Babylon, with houses, gardens and work — exactly as Jeremiah had advised them (Jeremiah 29:5). To them Jerusalem was a ruined city they had never seen.

The text does **not condemn** those who stayed. Not one word. That is worth noticing exactly.

**Forty-two Thousand People**

Those who went got a long list. Ezra chapter 2 is full of names, families and towns. At the end comes a number: **forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty** (2:64).

The list also has a sad entry (2:59): there were some who came up **but could not show their family and their descent.** The exile had been long. Documents were lost. Memories blurred.

And the text does not send them away. It does not even decide about them. It says: let this question stay open until a priest can rule on it (2:63). It **leaves a question open.** This book does that calmly.

**The Altar First**

They arrived. Now what do you do with a ruined city?

They did not build the wall first. Not the houses. Not the temple.

The first thing they built was an **altar** (3:2) — a pile of stones where an offering can be made. And 3:6 says exactly what that meant: *they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, but the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not yet been laid.*

There was no temple. Only an altar, under open sky, among the ruins. And they had already begun.

But 3:3 adds something it does not prettify: *they set the altar on its site, for **fear** was upon them because of the surrounding peoples.*

They did not begin in triumph. They began afraid.

**The Foundation Stone**

Then came the great day. They laid the foundation of the temple.

They stationed the priests with trumpets and the Levites with cymbals, according to David's old order (3:10). And they sang — the song Israel had sung for centuries:

*For he is good, for his love toward Israel endures for ever* (3:11).

And all the people **shouted with great joy.**

**But Not Everyone Shouted**

And here comes the heart of this part, the thing that makes the whole journey here worth it.

There were old people there. Priests, Levites, heads of families who had **seen the first house** — Solomon's temple, before Nebuchadnezzar tore it down. Seventy years ago. In their childhood.

They saw this foundation, and they **wept aloud** (3:12).

Why? Because it was small. Because they remembered something greater. Because they knew what had been lost.

And the others — the young, who had only heard about the first house — **shouted for joy.** Because for them this was the greatest thing that had ever happened.

**One Sound**

Now read 3:13, because it is one of the most beautiful verses in the Bible:

*So that the people could not tell the sound of the shout of joy from the sound of the weeping of the people, for the people shouted with a great shout, and the sound was heard far away.*

They could not be told apart. Anyone listening from outside heard one great sound and could not have said whether it was joy or grief.

And here is the most important thing: the text does **not correct those who wept.** It does not say they were ungrateful. It does not say they failed to understand what was happening. It does not say they should stop.

It does not say which sound was the right one.

Because sometimes both are right. You can rejoice over a beginning and weep over what was lost in the very same minute. The Bible knows this, and it does not ask you to choose.

**Two Neighbouring Books, Two Methods**

If we have only just finished the book of Esther, the opening sentence of Ezra is almost startling:

*In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus, so that the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah might be fulfilled* (1:1).

The book of Esther, over thirty-three pages, **never once** named God, and never once gave a cause for any of its turns. Even at the sleepless night, 6:1 supplied no subject: *the king's sleep fled* (p34).

Ezra 1:1 names the actor in the first half of the sentence and the purpose in the second: the word of Jeremiah.

Neither method is better than the other. The canon kept both — side by side.

**The Seventy Years, and What Is Difficult About Them**

Which word does 1:1 point to? Jeremiah spoke of seventy years twice:
- **Jeremiah 25:11-12** — this land will become a waste, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years
- **Jeremiah 29:10** — when the seventy years are completed, I will visit you and bring you back to this place

And now the honest part: **the counting of the seventy years is not obvious,** and the text does not give the arithmetic.

Two possible countings, each with its supporters:
- **From 605 BC** (the first deportation, when Daniel too was taken, p24) **to 538** (Cyrus's decree) — about 67 years
- **From 586 BC** (the destruction of the temple) **to 516** (the completion of the second temple) — about 70 years

Both are defensible. It may be that seventy is a round number, as the Bible uses it elsewhere (the length of a human life in Psalm 90:10). It may be an exact figure for a start and end point the text does not name.

We do not know for certain. And anyone who says they know exactly is claiming more than the text gives.

**Cyrus — and What Must Not Be Read Into Him**

In 1:2 Cyrus speaks: *The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house in Jerusalem.*

A fine sentence. But what does it mean?

There is an object that tells us a great deal: the **Cyrus Cylinder.** A clay cylinder found in Babylon in 1879, now on display in the British Museum in London. It carries Cyrus's own text.

And what does it say? That Cyrus restored the ruined sanctuaries, sent the deported peoples home, and — note this — that all of it was entrusted to him by **Marduk,** the chief god of Babylon, who chose him and gave the city into his hand.

So the very sentence that Ezra 1:2 writes about the God of Israel, Cyrus also had written about **Marduk.**

Two things follow from this at once:

**1. The Bible's picture of the policy is accurate.** Cyrus really did pursue such a policy: he restored local sanctuaries and did it in the name of the god of the people concerned. This is confirmed from an outside source. That is serious corroboration.

**2. But Ezra 1:2 must NOT be read as Cyrus's personal faith.** The Bible does not say Cyrus believed in the God of Israel. It does not say he converted. It does not say he did it for them alone.

A good decision is not the same as a confession of faith. This has to be read precisely. (Isaiah 45:1, for that matter, calls Cyrus **anointed,** and 45:4-5 adds: *though you do not know me.* The Bible itself states that Cyrus did not know the God of Israel.)

**The Second Exodus**

1:4 asks for something strange: that those who stay behind **help** the returnees with silver, gold, goods and animals.

The wording is no accident. The same thing happened in Exodus 12:35-36: when Israel came out of Egypt, the Egyptians gave them **silver and gold.**

The book of Ezra presents the return as a **second exodus.** The same movement: coming out of an empire, laden with gifts, toward a promise.

**The List, and the Number That Does Not Add Up**

Ezra 2 is a long roll of names. At the end: *the whole assembly together was forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty* (2:64).

Now comes an honest difficulty that cannot be hidden.

If you add up the individual figures listed in the chapter, you get about **twenty-nine thousand eight hundred.** Not forty-two thousand.

And there is more: the same list appears **a second time** in the Bible, in **Nehemiah 7** — and there many individual figures are **different,** while the total is the same: forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty.

What can be said about this?

There are several explanations, none of them proven:
- the total includes people the list does not itemise (women, servants, those of uncertain descent mentioned in 2:59)
- because of the way Hebrew numerals could be written, figures changed easily in copying
- the two lists are registers made at two different times

But one thing is worth noticing: **the tradition preserved both lists.** It did not smooth them over. It did not harmonise them. Whoever gathered the Bible together saw the difference and **left it in.**

**The Question They Left Open**

2:59 reports a hard situation: some came up but could not show their descent. Over the seventy years of exile the documents were lost.

And what does the text do? By 2:63: the decision was deferred until a priest should rule on it with the **Urim and the Thummim** (the instruments of high-priestly decision).

So they **did not decide.** They did not exclude them, and they did not grant them full standing. They left it open.

This is the book's method too: leaving an open question open is more honest than closing it quickly.

**The Altar First, in Fear**

In 3:1 the people gathered to Jerusalem **as one man.** Then Jeshua (the high priest) and Zerubbabel (a leader of David's house) built the altar, *as it is written in the law of Moses* (3:2).

And 3:3 states the reason too: *for fear was upon them because of the surrounding peoples.*

This is no triumphal procession. The text itself names the fear — just as Esther 8:17 and 9:3 named fear (p35). These books do not make a heroic story out of what began in fear.

And 3:6 holds the key detail: *they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, **but the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not yet been laid.***

Altar first, temple later. Worship did not wait for the building.

**The Foundation Stone and the Two Sounds**

In 3:10 they laid the foundation and stationed the priests with trumpets and the Levites with cymbals, *according to the directions of David.*

And they sang (3:11): *For he is good, for his love toward Israel endures for ever.*

This refrain is not new. It is the refrain of **Psalm 136,** repeated through twenty-six verses; it frames Psalm 118 at its beginning and end; and 1 Chronicles 16:34 quotes it too. A people who for seventy years could not sing it in the temple now begin again — with the same line.

And 3:12: *many of the older priests, Levites and heads of families, who had seen the first house, wept aloud.*

**Haggai 2:3** asks about this same loss, at roughly the same time: *Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory?* Haggai also gives an answer there (2:9: the glory of this house will be greater).

But **Ezra 3 gives no answer.** It does not comfort. It does not explain. It simply records the two sounds and adds (3:13) that they could not be told apart.

**What the Text Does NOT Say**

Four things 3:12-13 does not say:
1. It does not say the older ones were wrong.
2. It does not say their weeping was unbelief.
3. It does not say they should stop.
4. **It does not say which sound was the right one.**

It simply lets both be there. And it lets the sound be **heard far away** — both of them in it.
story.h:
**What Changes When the Exile Ends?**

This part is one of the turning points of the whole journey. Until now a people lost everything and learned how to live on foreign soil. From here on they go back — and they discover that going back is not the same as getting it back.

Four things have to be discussed precisely: the seventy years, Cyrus, the numbers, and the two sounds.

**1. Ezra 1:1 — When the Bible States the Cause**

Coming straight out of the book of Esther (p31-p35), this sentence is almost a shock:

*The LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus.*

The Hebrew verb is *he'ir* — to rouse, to stir; the same verb stands in 1:5 about the returnees. The same verb for Cyrus and for the people of God. The text draws no distinction between them as to who set them in motion.

Compare the book of Esther. There:
- God's name does not appear (p35)
- In 6:1 the king's sleeplessness is **given no cause** — the Hebrew *nadeda* has no subject (p34)
- 4:14 is a **question,** not a statement: *who knows?* (p33)

Here, in the first half-sentence, the actor is named.

This does not mean one book is better. It means that **the Bible contains both stated and silent narration,** and the canon kept both. There are times when a person sees God's hand in their own story, times when they see it only afterwards, and times when they never see it. There is a book for all three.

**2. The Seventy Years — and the Arithmetic the Text Does Not Do**

1:1 points to Jeremiah. There are two places:
- **Jeremiah 25:11-12** — the land will become a waste, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years; and after the seventy years are completed I will judge the king of Babylon
- **Jeremiah 29:10** — when seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you

2 Chronicles 36:21 also points to this and adds another angle: the land was fulfilling its **years of rest** (the sabbath-year idea from Leviticus 26:34-35).

The difficulty: from when to when do we count?

**Three proposals, all three with scholarly support:**

| Start | End | Length | The event |
|---|---|---|---|
| 605 BC | 539/538 | about 67 yrs | first deportation (Dan 1:1) - Cyrus's victory |
| 597 BC | 538 | about 59 yrs | deportation of Jehoiachin - the decree |
| 586 BC | 516 | about 70 yrs | destruction of the temple - completion of the second temple |

The third yields seventy most exactly, but 2 Chronicles 36 seems to have the first or second in view, and Ezra 1:1 ties it to the first year of Cyrus.

There is a fourth possibility worth weighing: **seventy as a round number.** In the Bible seventy often marks completeness — the span of a life in Psalm 90:10, seventy nations in Genesis 10, seventy elders in Exodus 24:1. Read that way, the seventy years say: **one full lifetime.** Those who left did not come back. Those who came back were born there.

The text does not give the arithmetic. That is not a problem — it just must not be turned into a certainty.

**3. Cyrus — the Cylinder, and the Line Not to Cross**

This is the most important precision in this part.

**The object.** In 1879 Hormuzd Rassam found a clay cylinder in Babylon with an inscription in Akkadian. It is now in the British Museum and is known as the **Cyrus Cylinder.** It is dated to around 539 BC.

**What is on it.** Cyrus relates that after the capture of Babylon he:
- restored the ruined sanctuaries
- returned the displaced gods to their own places
- sent the deported populations home
- and that all of it was entrusted to him by **Marduk,** who chose him and gave the city into his hand

So the structure of the sentence we read in Ezra 1:2 — *the LORD, the God of heaven... he has charged me* — is a **known Persian court formula** that Cyrus used with other peoples' gods as well.

**What does this mean, and what does it not?**

**What is corroboration:** the policy the Bible describes is real. A biblical author did not invent the idea that a Persian king would send peoples home and have a temple built for them in the name of their own god. This is documented Persian practice. That is serious and important.

**What does not follow:** it does not follow that Cyrus believed in the God of Israel. And the Bible does not claim it either.

In fact the Bible says the opposite outright. Isaiah 45:1 calls Cyrus **the LORD's anointed** (in Hebrew *mashiach*), which is unique in the Bible for a foreign king. But 45:4-5 adds at once: *I call you by your name... **though you do not know me.***

So the Bible says at the same time that God used Cyrus and that Cyrus did not know him.

This is an important idea, and it is not only about Cyrus: **someone can do good, can be an instrument in something large, without having to make a confession of faith.** And in reverse: you cannot reverse-engineer what someone believes from one good decision.

Anyone who teaches Ezra 1:2 as Cyrus's conversion contradicts Isaiah 45:4.

**4. The Numbers — the Difficulty the Tradition Left In**

2:64 says: the whole assembly was **42,360.**

There are two problems, and neither is a secret:

**First: the itemised figures add up to less.** Adding up the groups listed in Ezra 2 gives about **29,818.** The missing twelve thousand and more is not explained in the chapter.

**Second: Nehemiah 7 gives the same list — with different details.** Nehemiah 7:6-72 is almost word for word the same roll, but **many individual figures differ** (for example the sons of Arah: 775 by Ezra 2:5, 652 by Nehemiah 7:10). The itemised figures in Nehemiah 7 add up to about **31,089.** And the total in both places is the same: **42,360.**

**Explanations, and how well each stands:**

1. **The total includes more than the items.** The list enumerates men by family and town; the total may include women, members of tribes not listed, and those of uncertain descent mentioned in 2:59. This is the most common explanation, but the text does not say it.
2. **Copying differences.** Hebrew numbers could also be written with letters, and similar letters were easily confused. This explains the differences between Ezra and Nehemiah, but it does not explain why the total nevertheless agrees.
3. **Two different registers.** One may have been made at the departure and the other after the arrival, with the numbers changing in between.

None is proven. The honest answer: **we do not know.**

But there is something here that is instructive in itself. The tradition **did not smooth the two lists out.** They stand side by side in the Bible with differing figures. Whoever edited these books together saw the difference — and **did not correct it.** That tells us something about how the Bible came to be: preservation mattered more than a smooth surface.

**5. 2:59-63 — When the Text Does Not Decide**

Some came up from Babylon but could not prove their descent (2:59). Among them were priestly families (2:61-62).

What happens to them? By 2:63 the leader said they were not to eat of the holy things until a priest should **stand up with the Urim and the Thummim.**

The Urim and the Thummim were instruments of high-priestly decision (Exodus 28:30; 1 Samuel 14:41; 28:6). And in the biblical record there is **no report** of their being used after the exile.

So 2:63 effectively means: the question **stays open, indefinitely.** They were not cut off from the people, and they did not receive full priestly rights.

This is not an evasion but a decision: not to close an uncertain question but to hold it open. The Bible does this elsewhere too (the question of Esther 4:14, p33; the sealed book of Daniel 12:8-9, p30).

**6. The Altar Before the Temple — and the Fear**

In 3:1 the people gathered **as one man** (in Hebrew *ke-ish echad*) — the same phrase as in Judges 20:1 and Nehemiah 8:1.

The seventh month is no accident: it holds the day of trumpet blasts, the great day of atonement and the festival of booths (Leviticus 23:23-43). The returnees began in the fullest month of the calendar.

And they built the altar first, *as it is written in the law of Moses* (3:2). Not the wall, not the houses, not the temple. 3:6 states it: *they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, but the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not yet been laid.*

But 3:3 gives the circumstance as well, and it must not be left out: *for **fear** was upon them because of the surrounding peoples.*

The text makes no heroic tale of this. No more than Esther 8:17 and 9:3 did, where fear was the named motive (p35). These books are precise about what moved people — and fear appears more often than triumph.

**7. The Two Sounds — the Heart of This Part**

In 3:10-11 they laid the foundation, the priests with trumpets, the Levites with cymbals, in David's order, and they sang: *for he is good, for his love toward Israel endures for ever.*

That refrain is the backbone of Psalm 136 (through twenty-six verses), the frame of Psalm 118, and 1 Chronicles 16:34 quotes it too. The text does not give them a new song. It gives back the **old** one.

And then 3:12. The older ones who had **seen the first house** wept aloud.

How old would someone have had to be? If the temple fell in 586 BC and the foundation was laid around 536, then anyone who remembered it had to be at least fifty-five or sixty. They had seen it as children. Seventy years before.

What did they see now? A foundation. Smaller. Poorer.

**Haggai 2:3** asks about this same moment (or very near it): *Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? And how does it look to you now?* Haggai also answers: by 2:9 *the glory of this latter house will be greater than the former.*

But **Ezra 3 gives no answer.** It does not quote Haggai. It does not comfort. It does not explain. It only records.

And 3:13: *the people could not tell the sound of the shout of joy from the sound of the weeping of the people.*

The Hebrew is emphatic: they could not *lehakkir* — recognise, identify. It was one sound.

**What 3:12-13 Does NOT Say — and Why It Matters**

Five things it does not say, and every absence is deliberate:

1. **It does not say the older ones were wrong.** Not one word suggests their weeping was improper.
2. **It does not say they lacked faith.** It does not say that with more trust they would not have wept.
3. **It does not say they should stop.** No one hushes them.
4. **It does not say there was anything wrong with the young people's joy.** Their shout is there too, with equal right.
5. **It does not say which sound was the right one.**

That absence is the verse's teaching. Because if the text had decided, someone would have had to lie about what they felt.

This speaks to those who read it as well. Sometimes a person stands in a good thing — a new school, a new home, a new beginning — and it still aches for what was lost. And sometimes they are expected to choose: either be glad or be sad.

Ezra 3:13 does not ask that. It says: **the two sounds ran together, and the sound was heard far away.**

Both were in it.

**What Comes Next?**

In p37 the work stops. Not because they grew tired — but because someone comes who asks nicely, and behind the asking is something else. And that is where Haggai and Zechariah come in, the two prophets who spoke into that standstill.
