story.e:
**A Hard Part — and One Important Thing First**

This is one of the hardest parts of the whole journey. Not because it is complicated, but because it is **sad,** and because it is about families.

So I will say something **first,** and I will not forget it at the end either:

In these two chapters there is **not one single place** where it says *thus says the LORD.* There is no divine command in them. What the people decided, **people** thought up, people voted for, and the book **does not say it was right.**

And one more thing: this chapter **can never, for anyone, be a reason** to send away a member of their family. If someone reads that out of it, they are not reading the Bible.

**The News**

Ezra arrived in Jerusalem (p39), handed over the treasure and offered sacrifice. Everything was in order.

Then the leaders came to him and told him something that shook him badly (9:1): that the people, the priests and the Levites **had not separated themselves** from the surrounding peoples and their practices.

Behind their fear was this: before the exile everything had been lost precisely because they lost what set them apart. Now, seventy years later, they were only a few thousand. And they believed that if it happened again, there would be no one left to remember.

**What Ezra Did — and What He Did Not**

Now comes the part worth noticing.

Ezra **had the right to punish.** The king's letter (7:26) said he could appoint judges, and that whoever did not keep the law could have judgement executed on him, even the gravest.

And what did he do with that authority?

**Nothing.**

9:3: *When I heard this, **I tore my garment** and my cloak, and sat down appalled.*

He sat down on the ground. And he sat there — not for a minute, but **until the evening sacrifice** (9:4), that is, for hours, without a word.

And others gathered to him too: *all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel.* They did not speak. They were simply there with him.

**The Prayer**

Then at the time of the evening sacrifice he rose, spread out his hands and prayed. And this prayer is not what you would expect.

He did not say: *My God, punish them.*

He said (9:6): *My God, **I am ashamed** and abashed to lift up my face to you, for our sins have risen higher than our heads.*

**Our sins.** Not *their sins.* Ezra **counted himself in** — though he had only just arrived and had nothing to do with it.

And then he said something beautiful (9:9): *For we are servants; yet **in our servitude our God has not forsaken us.***

And 9:13: *you have punished us **less** than our sins deserved.*

**The Prayer That Asks for Nothing**

And now notice the strangest thing of all.

This prayer **has no request.**

It does not close with *forgive us.* Not with *help us.* Not with *tell us what to do.*

Its last words are these (9:15): *Behold, **we are before you** in our guilt.*

And that is it. That is all. Nothing follows.

Sometimes a prayer is just this much: we are here, and we say no more.

**The People Weep**

And while Ezra was praying like this, *weeping and prostrate before the house of God,* something happened (10:1):

*A very great assembly gathered to him from Israel: **men, women and children;** for the people wept bitterly too.*

One man's grief moved a whole people.

**The Proposal — and Whom It Came From**

And now a very important detail.

The **proposal did not come from Ezra.** There is not one proposal in Ezra's prayer. He did not say what should be done.

A man spoke out of the crowd: **Shecaniah** (10:2). He said: *We have sinned against our God; yet now **there is hope** for Israel.*

And he made the proposal (10:3), and he said to Ezra (10:4): *Rise up, for this matter is yours, and we are with you; be strong and do it!*

So the people decided, and asked Ezra to lead it.

**The Rain**

Within three days everyone gathered to Jerusalem. And 10:9 records something a book usually does not record:

*All the people sat in the square, **trembling because of the rain.***

This was the tenth month — the middle of the Jerusalem rainy season. Cold, wet, miserable. And the book puts that in too.

And the people themselves said (10:13): *the people are many, and it is the rainy season, and we cannot stand out here; and this is **not the work of one or two days.***

**Those Who Did Not Consent**

And now something very unusual in an ancient book.

10:15: *But **Jonathan** son of Asahel and **Jahzeiah** son of Tikvah opposed this, and **Meshullam** and **Shabbethai** the Levite supported them.*

Four men's **names** are there, men who did not consent.

And the book **does not condemn them.** It does not say they were guilty. It does not say they were wrong. It only records that there were those who thought differently — and it keeps their names.

**The End of the Book**

The examination lasted three months (10:16-17). Then the book lists the names.

And its **last verse** is this (10:44):

*All these had taken foreign wives; and there were among them some **who also had children.***

And there the book ends.

Nothing follows. No *and everything turned out well.* No *and God was pleased.* No *and so it was right.*

The book stops in the middle of a sentence about children — and **says nothing about what became of them.**

**What to Take from This**

This is one of the bleakest endings in the Bible. And the Bible left it that way **deliberately.**

It does not say God commanded it. It does not say it was right. It does not say it ended well.

It kept **the fear** (a people who believed they were disappearing), it kept **the grief** (Ezra's and the people's weeping), it kept **the dissent** (four names), and it kept **the children in the last sentence.**

And in that same Bible stands the **book of Ruth** — about a Moabite woman who became an ancestress of king David. And in it stands **Malachi 2:16,** from this very same period, which speaks **against sending away.**

So the Bible does not speak with one voice about this. And anyone who would use this chapter to exclude or send someone away **runs against the rest of the Bible.**
story.m:
**To Be Said First**

Before I say anything about these two chapters, I will state three things, because without them everything that follows can be misread:

1. In Ezra 9-10 **there is not one place** where it says *thus says the LORD.* Not one divine command.
2. The decision **did not begin with Ezra.** One man, **Shecaniah,** proposed it, and a human assembly carried it out.
3. The book **does not say this was right.** It stops, and it passes no verdict.

This is not an evasion. It is the text itself.

**9:1-2 — The Report**

The leaders reported to Ezra that the people *had not separated themselves from the surrounding peoples and their practices* (9:1).

What was at stake? This is worth understanding, because without it the chapter is unintelligible.

The returned community was **very small.** Forty-two thousand people came back in the first wave (p36), and Jerusalem and its surroundings were a small, poor, wall-less province in a great empire. Around it, many larger peoples.

And the community believed — on the basis of their own prophets (see the confession of 5:12, p38) — that the exile had happened because they lost what set them apart. So their fear was this: **if it happens again, there will be no one left to remember.**

This does not justify the decision. But it explains the fear, and without the fear this chapter cannot be understood.

**9:3-5 — The Reaction, and What He Did NOT Do**

Ezra **had judicial authority.** In 7:25-26 Artaxerxes had written: appoint judges, and whoever does not keep the law, let judgement be executed on him — by death, banishment, confiscation or imprisonment (p39).

And what did he do with that authority when he heard the news?

**Nothing.** He summoned no judges. He ordered no inquiry. He passed no sentence.

9:3: *I tore my garment and my cloak, and sat down appalled.*

The Hebrew word is *meshomem* — appalled, stunned, literally: turned to stone. The same word stands in Daniel 8:27 for Daniel's state after the vision.

And 9:4: *I sat appalled until the **evening sacrifice.*** That is, for hours, motionless, without a word.

So the book shows us a man who had authority, and who **sat down on the ground.**

**9:6-15 — The Prayer, and Three Things in It**

At the evening sacrifice he rose and prayed. Three things are worth noticing.

**The first: the pronouns.**

9:6: *our sins have risen higher than our heads.*
9:7: *from the days of our fathers **we** have been in great guilt.*
9:13: *after all that has come upon **us** for **our** evil deeds.*

Ezra had just arrived from Babylon. He had nothing to do with this. And still he says **we,** throughout.

This is the same move as in Daniel 9:5 (*we have sinned, we have done wrong*) — and there too the speaker is a man of whom the book records no fault.

**The second: the balance.**

9:8-9 speaks of grace: *for a brief moment we have received grace... that he might leave us a remnant... for we are servants; **yet in our servitude our God has not forsaken us.***

And 9:13: *you have punished us **less** than our sins deserved.*

Ezra is not speaking of injustice. He says they received less than they expected.

**The third, and this is the most important: the prayer has no petition.**

Read 9:15: *O LORD, God of Israel, you are just; for a remnant of us is left, as it is this day. **Behold, we are before you in our guilt,** for no one can stand before you because of this.*

And there the prayer **ends.**

No *forgive.* No *help.* No *tell us what to do.* No *cleanse us.*

This is unusual. Biblical prayers of confession (Daniel 9, Nehemiah 9, Psalm 51) usually close with a **petition.** This one does not.

What does that mean? The text does not say. But one thing it certainly means: **Ezra's prayer contains no plan.** It proposes nothing. It does not say what should be done.

That is decisive, because in the next chapter there will be a plan — and **it does not come from Ezra.**

**10:1 — The People**

*While Ezra was praying and making confession, weeping and prostrate before the house of God, a very great assembly gathered to him from Israel: **men, women and children;** for the people wept bitterly too.*

Notice who is there: *men, women and children.* The book places the whole people there.

**10:2-4 — Shecaniah, and Where the Proposal Comes From**

And now the most important structural fact of this part.

The proposal comes from **Shecaniah,** not from Ezra.

10:2: *And **Shecaniah** spoke and said to Ezra: We have sinned against our God; **yet now there is hope** for Israel in this matter.*

10:3: the proposal.

10:4: *Rise up, for **this matter is yours,** and we are with you; be strong and do it!*

So: a man out of the assembly comes forward with a proposal, and **hands the execution over** to the leader. Ezra initiated nothing. He prayed, and the people came to him.

And a detail that gives one pause: Shecaniah is **son of Jehiel** (10:2) — and in 10:26 a **Jehiel** appears in the list of those who had taken a foreign wife.

Could it be the same family? **It is possible, even likely** — but the text **does not say so.** If it is, then Shecaniah made a proposal that touched his own family too. That would explain why he was the one who spoke. But this is an inference, not the text's claim.

**10:3 — According to the Law — and What Does Not Fit Here**

Shecaniah says (10:3): *let it be done **according to the law.***

According to which law?

The places usually cited: **Deuteronomy 7:1-4** and **Exodus 34:15-16.** Both **forbid** making such a marriage.

But now notice: **neither commands the dissolving of marriages already made.** A prohibition and a dissolution are not the same thing.

So Shecaniah's proposal **goes beyond** what it appeals to. We will go into this in detail on the hard level, because it is the most important fact about this chapter.

**10:9-14 — The Square and the Rain**

Everyone gathered within three days. And the book gives two details a triumphant narrative would leave out:

**10:9:** *all the people sat in the square, **trembling because of the rain.*** The tenth month is the middle of the Jerusalem rainy season (December-January).

**10:13:** and the people themselves speak: *the people are many, and it is the rainy season, and we cannot stand out here; and this is **not the work of one or two days,** for we are many who have sinned in this.*

And the people propose something (10:14): that the leaders should stand in place of the assembly, and the rest come from their own towns at appointed times. That is: **not one great collective decision, but examination case by case.**

That matters. The people themselves asked that the decision not be made quickly and all together.

**10:15 — The Recorded Dissent**

*But **Jonathan** son of Asahel and **Jahzeiah** son of Tikvah opposed this, and **Meshullam** and **Shabbethai** the Levite supported them.*

Four names. Four men who did not consent.

And the text **does not condemn them.** It does not call them unfaithful, does not say they were wrong, says nothing about them at all.

An ancient book describing a communal decision **kept the names of those who spoke against it.** That is very unusual.

(A note: the Hebrew of 10:15 is slightly open, and a few translations render it as though these men **supported** the matter. Most modern translations and the most probable reading, however, are opposition — because the construction *stood against this* elsewhere in the Bible marks opposition.)

**10:16-44 — The Examination and the End**

The examination began on the first day of the tenth month (10:16) and lasted until the first day of the first month (10:17) — **about three months.** Not one day, not one assembly. Examination case by case.

Then the book lists the names, and its **very last verse** is this (10:44):

*All these had taken foreign wives; and there were among them some **who also had children.***

And with that the book **ends.**

No closure. No assessment. No *and so it was well.* No *and God accepted it.* Not one word about what became of the women and the children.

The book **stops** at the point where children are mentioned.

**What the Hard Level Brings**

On the next level four things have to be said: what the law says and does not say; that Nehemiah handled this same problem **differently;** what stands in this same Bible as its opposite; and that this chapter can **never** be a reason for sending anyone away from their family.
story.h:
**Before Anything Else**

This is one of the hardest parts of the whole journey, and the only one where it is necessary to state in advance how it must **not** be used.

I begin with four facts, all four of them checkable in the text:

1. In Ezra 9-10 it **never once** says *thus says the LORD,* or *the LORD commanded.* Zero occurrences. There is no divine word in these two chapters.
2. The decision **did not come from Ezra.** In his prayer (9:6-15) there is **not one proposal,** and the prayer closes **without a petition.** The proposal comes from Shecaniah (10:2-4).
3. The law Shecaniah appeals to **forbids** such a marriage, but **does not command** the dissolving of ones already made.
4. The book **passes no verdict** on the outcome. It stops at the last verse and says not a word about whether this was right.

And from that follows the most important thing to say:

**This chapter can never, for anyone, be a reason to send away a member of their family, or to exclude anyone from a community because of their descent.** Whoever uses it that way is not passing on the Bible's content but an ancient human decision made in fear — one that the Bible itself never called right.

Now let us look precisely at what stands in the text.

**1. The Fear, Without Which It Is Unintelligible**

I set this out not to justify, but because without the fear this chapter cannot be read.

The returned community was small. Forty-two thousand in the first wave (p36), still only some tens of thousands eighty years later, in a poor province without walls (the walls come in p41).

And the community's conviction — from their own prophets, and from their own confession in 5:12 (p38) — was that the exile had happened because the people lost what set them apart. 9:13-14 states exactly this: *after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds... shall we break your commandments again?*

So their fear was: **if this repeats, there will be no one to remember.** It was not a theoretical fear. The ten northern tribes had vanished from history in exactly this way eighty years earlier (2 Kings 17).

A people who believed they could disappear made a decision that a people living in safety would never have made. That explains the decision. It **does not justify** it.

**2. The Question of Descent — and Facts That Stand Together**

Now a point that must not be simplified.

**9:1-2 names descent.** The verse lists the peoples, and 9:2 says that *the holy seed has mixed itself with the peoples of the land.* This language is uncomfortable, and the modern reader's unease is **not a misreading.**

**But that same Bible contains:**

- The **book of Ruth** — Ruth is a Moabite woman (Ruth 1:4), and at the end of the book it turns out that she became **an ancestress of king David** (Ruth 4:17-22). And Deuteronomy 23:4 contains a prohibition about Moabites.
- The story of **Rahab** — a Canaanite woman from Jericho (Joshua 2; 6:25) who joined Israel.
- **Zipporah,** Moses' wife — a Midianite woman (Exodus 2:21); and when Miriam and Aaron objected to Moses' wife, **God rebuked them** (Numbers 12).
- **Isaiah 56:3-8** — *let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say: the LORD has separated me from his people... my house shall be a house of prayer for all peoples.*
- And — most decisive of all — **Ezra 6:21,** in this very book: those who had returned ate the Passover *together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD* (p38).

Ezra 6:21 is decisive because it is **the same book.** So the book of Ezra itself does not treat descent as the boundary, but whether someone *seeks the LORD.*

What can we honestly say from this? That the **Bible does not speak with one voice about this,** and that chapters 9-10 are **not the canon's position** on the question but a specific measure in a specific situation. Anyone who makes a general rule out of 9:2 has to contend with the book of Ruth, Isaiah 56 and Ezra 6:21.

**3. The Most Important Factual Question: What Does the Law Command?**

Shecaniah says (10:3): *let it be done according to the law.*

Let us look at what that law says.

**Deuteronomy 7:1-4** — when you enter the land, make no covenant with those peoples, and **do not give your daughter to their son, and do not take their daughter for your son.**

**Exodus 34:15-16** — make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and **do not take their daughters** for your sons.

What do these two places say? **A prohibition on contracting such marriage.**

What do they **not** say? Not one word about dissolving marriages **already made,** and not one word about sending children away.

This is not a small detail. It is the most important fact about this chapter:

**The measure goes beyond the law it appeals to.**

The Torah does, incidentally, have a rule about what must be done if a man sends away his wife (Deuteronomy 24:1-4), and a rule protecting a woman taken as a captive of war (Deuteronomy 21:10-14) — where it explicitly **forbids** selling her for money. So the Torah is not simply silent on the question; it has protective rules that this measure does not apply.

**4. Nehemiah with the Same Problem — a Different Solution**

And now comes the strongest argument that this measure was not God's command.

A few decades later **Nehemiah** meets the same problem. In **Nehemiah 13:23-27** he records that he saw the mixed marriages from Ashdod, Moab and Ammon, and that the children could no longer speak the language of Judah.

What did he do?

13:25: *I rebuked them and cursed them and beat some of them and pulled out their hair, and **made them swear** by God: do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take their daughters.*

So Nehemiah:
- **took an oath** about the future
- and in 13:28 **sent one man away** (a priest who had become the son-in-law of Sanballat of Samaria)
- but **did not order** a general sending away of existing families

The same problem. The same period. The same community. **Two entirely different measures.**

And the Bible calls **neither** of them God's command, and condemns **neither.**

If this had been God's unambiguous command, it could not have been carried out in two different ways. So the Bible itself shows that this was a **human decision** — two human answers to the same fear.

**5. Malachi — a Prophetic Word in This Same Period**

And now something that again comes from this same time.

The book of **Malachi** can with high probability be dated precisely to this period (the second temple is standing, the priestly service is weakening, there is no king). And Malachi 2:14-16 speaks about a man **sending away his wife:**

2:14: *the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have forsaken, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant.*

2:16: *for I hate sending away, says the LORD, the God of Israel... and the one who covers his garment with violence.*

(A precision: the Hebrew of 2:16 is difficult, and translations differ. Some read *I hate divorce,* others *whoever divorces, I hate him,* others again *whoever hates, divorces.* But on every reading the sentence speaks **against** sending away, not for it.)

Notice the difference: in Malachi 2:16 it **is** there, *thus says the LORD.* In Ezra 9-10 it is **not.**

So in the same period, in the same canon, the Bible set a **prophetic word** against sending away — with God's name on it — while it left the human decision of Ezra 9-10 without God's name.

I am not the one assembling this. **The canon assembled it that way.**

**6. What Ezra Did — and What He Did Not**

Four things that speak for Ezra, and these too have to be said:

**First: he did not use his judicial authority.** By 7:25-26 he could have punished, even with death (p39). On hearing the news he summoned no judge but **sat down on the ground** and sat until the evening sacrifice (9:3-4). In the book **we read of no execution at all.**

**Second: he counted himself in.** His prayer speaks in **we** throughout (9:6, 9:7, 9:13), though he had only just arrived. He did not stand outside.

**Third: his prayer contains no plan.** This is checkable: read 9:6-15 and you will find no proposal. The prayer closes **without a petition:** *behold, we are before you in our guilt* (9:15). Biblical prayers of confession (Daniel 9:19, Nehemiah 9:32, Psalm 51:3) usually close with a petition. **This one does not.**

**Fourth: he was not the one who proposed it.** The proposal came from Shecaniah (10:2-3), and **he was the one who told Ezra** that *this matter is yours* (10:4).

None of this means Ezra was not responsible for the execution — he was. It means the text is **precise** about who initiated what, and that must not be blurred.

**7. The Four Names Who Did Not Consent**

10:15: *But Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah **opposed** this, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite supported them.*

This verse is remarkable in itself. An ancient communal record **kept the names of those who spoke against it** — and did not qualify them with a single word.

It does not call them unfaithful. It does not say they repented later. It does not say God punished them. They are simply **there,** with four names.

An honest textual note: the Hebrew construction (*amdu al-zot*) literally means *they stood against this,* and could in principle mean support (*they stood up in this matter*). A few old translations rendered it that way. But most modern translations and the most probable reading are **opposition,** because the preposition *al* in this construction marks opposition elsewhere in the Bible, and because the verse begins with *but,* signalling contrast.

What we can say for certain: **the book recorded that it was not unanimous.**

**8. The Last Verse, and an Ancient Trace**

The book's last verse (10:44): *All these had taken foreign wives; and there were among them some who also had children.*

And here the book **stops.**

No closure. The historical books of ancient Israel usually close with some assessment — 2 Kings with the release of Jehoiachin, 2 Chronicles with the decree of Cyrus. The book of Ezra closes with an **unfinished sentence** about children.

And here is an interesting ancient trace showing that **old readers also found this verse hard.**

There is a Greek book we call **1 Esdras** (part of the Septuagint, not in the Catholic or Protestant canons). It is broadly a Greek retelling of the book of Ezra. And 1 Esdras 9:36 closes like this: *and they sent them away **together with their children.***

So the Greek text **added** half a sentence — supplying the closure the Hebrew did not supply. This proves nothing about what happened. But it shows that **even in antiquity people felt this verse was unfinished,** and someone tried to finish it.

The Hebrew text did not finish it. And the canon kept the Hebrew text.

**9. What Did the Bible Do with This? — the Decisive Question**

Let us sum up what the Bible **did** with this story:

| What it did | What it did NOT do |
|---|---|
| It recorded the fear | It did not call it God's command |
| It recorded Ezra's grief | It did not say it was right |
| It kept who the proposal came from | It did not say God gave the proposal |
| It kept the four dissenters' names | It did not condemn them |
| It recorded the rain and the trembling | It made no triumph out of it |
| It mentioned the children | It did not say what became of them |

This is the same method with which **Esther chapter 9** handled its hard passage (p35), and with which **Daniel 6:25** quoted the king's decree (p29): **it reports, it does not command.**

The module has repeated this finding throughout, and here it is sharpest: **what the Bible records is not the same as what it teaches.**

**10. And Now the Point — What Cannot Be Done with This**

I close this part with a plain sentence, because this is the most important thing in the whole of it.

This chapter has often served as a pretext in history. It has been used for racial theories, used to exclude people, used to break up marriages.

Every such use makes the same error: **it turns a recorded human decision into a command.**

And every such use runs against:
- **The book of Ruth** (a Moabite woman, ancestress of David)
- **Isaiah 56:3-8** (let not the foreigner who joined say he was separated)
- **Ezra 6:21** (the same book!)
- **Malachi 2:14-16** (the same period, with God's name, against sending away)
- **The Torah's commands about the stranger, the widow and the orphan** (Exodus 22:21-22; Deuteronomy 10:18-19; 24:17)
- And the New Testament word: *there is neither Jew nor Greek... for you are all one* (Galatians 3:28), and Jesus' genealogy, which **names four women of foreign descent:** Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah (Matthew 1:3-6)

That last is the most telling. When Matthew writes the genealogy of Jesus, he names four women — and all four came **from outside.** A Canaanite, a Moabite, and two whose stories are scandalous.

If Ezra 9-10 had been the last word, those names would not be there.

**What Comes Next?**

In p41 a new man comes, and new work: **Nehemiah,** a court official who receives news about the walls of Jerusalem. And we will see that he decides differently from Ezra — more than once — and that the Bible kept that too.

verse.text: For we are servants; yet in our servitude our God has not forsaken us.

bio.hu: Dávid őt állította az éneklők élére, és tizenkét zsoltár viseli a nevét. Nem szép szavakat írt: az egyik zsoltárában bevallja, hogy majdnem megcsúszott a lába, mert látta, milyen jól megy a gőgösöknek. Nem titkolta el ezt a haragot — leírta, és úgy vitte Isten elé. Az ő énekes utódai még hetven évvel később, a hazatérés után is ott álltak és énekeltek.
bio.en: David put him in charge of the singers, and twelve psalms bear his name. He did not write pretty words: in one of his psalms he admits that his feet almost slipped, because he saw how well things went for the proud. He did not hide that anger — he wrote it down and brought it to God that way. His singer descendants were still standing and singing seventy years later, after the return home.

How many psalms bear Asaph's name?

What troubled Asaph?
o: That things went well for the proud
That he had too few singers
That he was not invited to the palace

o: He wrote it down and brought it to God

o: When he went into God's sanctuary
When he received a new song

Only a cheerful person may pray

bio.hu: Három fiú, akiket Dániellel együtt hurcoltak el, és még a nevüket is elvették tőlük. Amikor a király hatalmas arany szobrot állított, és a zenére mindenkinek le kellett borulnia, ők állva maradtak. A mondatuk a történet lelke: van Istenünk, aki meg tud szabadítani — de ha nem szabadít meg, akkor sem szolgáljuk a te isteneidet. Megkötözve estek a tűzbe, és a király négy embert látott benne járkálni.
bio.en: Three boys carried off together with Daniel, who even had their names taken from them. When the king set up a huge golden statue and everyone had to bow down at the music, they stayed standing. Their sentence is the heart of the story: we have a God who can rescue us — but if he does not rescue us, we still will not serve your gods. They fell into the fire tied up, and the king saw four men walking about in it.

hu.q: Mit vettek el a három fiútól a fogságban?

en.q: What was taken from the three boys in exile?
What did the king set up?

bio.hu: Zsidó ember Súsán várában, aki a szülők nélkül maradt Esztert felnevelte. Egyszer leleplezett egy összeesküvést a király ellen, és feljegyezték a könyvbe — de évekig semmit nem kapott érte. Hámán előtt nem hajolt meg, és ezért az egész népét veszélybe hozta. Nem hallgatott: gyászruhát vett, és ő üzente Eszternek a kérdést, ami az egész könyv fordulópontja.
bio.en: A Jewish man in the fortress of Susa who raised Esther when she was left without parents. Once he uncovered a plot against the king, and it was written in the book — but for years he received nothing for it. He would not bow before Haman, and so brought his whole people into danger. He did not keep silent: he put on mourning clothes, and it was he who sent Esther the question that turns the whole book.

hu.q: Mit tett, amikor meghallotta a nép elleni rendeletet?

en.q: What did he do when he heard the decree against his people?
o: He put on mourning clothes and ashes
He went to the palace shouting
Ki tudja, nem ezért az időért jutottál-e oda?

en.q: What message did he send Esther?
o: Who knows whether you came to this place for such a time?

Ki kell mondani, amit látunk, akkor is, ha veszélyes

en.q: What does Mordecai's story teach?

It is better not to speak

bio.hu: Héber neve Hadassza volt. Nem ő döntött úgy, hogy a palotába megy: elvitték. Évekig titkolta, hogy zsidó. Amikor az egész népe veszélybe került, három napos böjtöt kért, és hívatlanul bement a királyhoz, pedig ezért halál járt. Ennyit mondott: ha elveszek, elveszek. Isten neve a könyvben egyetlenegyszer sem szerepel — mégis minden megfordul.
bio.en: Her Hebrew name was Hadassah. It was not her choice to go to the palace: she was taken. For years she kept hidden that she was Jewish. When her whole people came into danger she asked for a three-day fast and went in to the king uninvited, though that carried the death penalty. She said only this: if I perish, I perish. God's name never appears once in the book — yet everything turns around.

bio.hu: A perzsa király pohárnoka volt — jó állás, biztonságos élet. Amikor meghallotta, hogy Jeruzsálem falai romokban állnak, leült és napokig sírt, böjtölt, imádkozott. Aztán megrémült a király előtt, de mégis kért: engedélyt, fát, leveleket. Éjjel egyedül körüljárta a romokat, és ötvenkét nap alatt felépült a fal. Egyik kezükben a szerszám, a másikban a fegyver.
bio.en: He was cupbearer to the Persian king — a good post and a safe life. When he heard that the walls of Jerusalem lay in ruins he sat down and wept for days, fasting and praying. Then he was terrified before the king, yet he asked anyway: for permission, for timber, for letters. At night he rode around the ruins alone, and in fifty-two days the wall was finished. A tool in one hand, a weapon in the other.

bio.hu: Pap és írástudó, aki egy egész csoportot vezetett haza Babilonból. Nem kért katonai kíséretet az útra, inkább böjtöt rendelt. Róla azt írja a Biblia, hogy szívből törekedett arra, hogy kutassa, megtegye és tanítsa Isten törvényét — ebben a sorrendben. A nagy téren hajnaltól délig olvasta fel a könyvet, és a léviták elmagyarázták, hogy a nép értse is, amit hall.
bio.en: A priest and scribe who led a whole group home from Babylon. He did not ask for a military escort for the journey; he called a fast instead. The Bible says of him that he set his heart to study, to do and to teach God's law — in that order. In the great square he read the book aloud from dawn until noon, and the Levites explained it so that the people would also understand what they heard.
